links.why: The sounds in the after-hold get their explanation: Fedallah and the phantom crew.
The First Lowering is where what is hidden below comes on deck.

ch44.essay:
Ahab at his charts, under a lamp that swings with the ship and throws lines across his forehead so that 'some invisible pencil was also tracing lines and courses upon the deeply marked chart of his forehead.' That image is the chapter for me: the man mapping the ocean is being mapped. Melville then does the thing he does best — makes the mad plan reasonable. Sperm whales follow currents and seasons and swim in 'veins' with a surveyor's precision; a chart of their migrations was actually being compiled in Washington (the footnote cites Lieutenant Maury, April 1851, the year the book came out). So finding one whale in the world's oceans is not absurd. It's a matter of collating logbooks and waiting for the Season-on-the-Line. Ahab's method is sound; only, again, the object is mad.

What I hadn't noticed on first reading is the last paragraph, which is one of the strangest passages in the novel. Ahab bursts from his stateroom at night with a cry, as though escaping a burning bed — and Ishmael argues that the thing fleeing is not Ahab's purpose but Ahab's soul, which in sleep dissociates from the monomaniac mind and runs from it in horror. The purpose has become 'a kind of self-assumed, independent being of its own' that can live and burn while the man's ordinary vitality flees it. So the figure that glares out of the cabin door is 'a vacated thing,' a ray of light with no object to color. Ahab has created a creature inside himself, and it feeds on him: Prometheus, and the vulture, both.

It's worth pausing on because it's the book's most explicit account of what obsession does. Not that Ahab wants revenge, but that the wanting has become a separate organism with its own life, and the man is its host.

The Chart's method — reason applied wholly to an insane end — is the 'sane means, mad object' that [[ch41:calm orders|the previous chapter]] diagnosed; and the instrument he trusts here, the chart, is what he will curse and stamp on in [[ch118|The Quadrant]].

annotations.quote: some invisible pencil was also tracing lines and courses upon the deeply marked chart of his forehead.
annotations.note: The chart-maker charted. The swinging lamp does it, physically, and the sentence lets you feel that Ahab's plans are being written on him as much as by him.

annotations.quote: Ahab was threading a maze of currents and eddies, with a view to the more certain accomplishment of that monomaniac thought of his soul.
annotations.note: The phrase 'more certain accomplishment' is bureaucratic, and that's the horror. Monomania here is not raving but project management — patient, nightly, revised in pencil.

annotations.quote: Since the above was written, the statement is happily borne out by an official circular, issued by Lieutenant Maury, of the National Observatory, Washington, April 16th, 1851.
annotations.note: A real footnote citing a real whale-migration chart from the year of publication. Melville wants you to know Ahab's method is state of the art. The fiction is anchored to a government document.

annotations.quote: guided by some infallible instinct—say, rather, secret intelligence from the Deity—mostly swim in _veins_
annotations.note: Whales follow lines straighter than any ship can steer. Ishmael's aside — 'say, rather, secret intelligence from the Deity' — is the kind of half-serious upgrade from instinct to revelation that keeps this book from being either science or sermon.

annotations.quote: He sleeps with clenched hands; and wakes with his own bloody nails in his palms.
annotations.note: Stigmata, self-inflicted. Ahab wounds himself in his sleep with his own grip. It's the physical cost of a will that never relaxes, and it's a Christ image turned inside out.

annotations.quote: that purpose, by its own sheer inveteracy of will, forced itself against gods and devils into a kind of self-assumed, independent being of its own.
annotations.note: The obsession has become a separate creature living in Ahab. This is the most precise thing the book says about monomania — the wanting has detached from the wanter and now runs the body.

annotations.quote: God help thee, old man, thy thoughts have created a creature in thee; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus; a vulture feeds upon that heart for ever; that vulture the very creature he creates.
annotations.note: Prometheus and his vulture as the same person. Ishmael's pity here is real — 'God help thee, old man' — and it's the pity the rest of the ship can't afford to feel.

links.why: The diagnosis this chapter illustrates: intact intellect in the service of the fixed idea.
Ahab destroying the quadrant is the end of the road the charts begin — science kept only as long as it serves.
The 'chasm opening in him' here is what Ahab finally speaks of aloud to Starbuck.

ch45.essay:
Ishmael turns lawyer. Having told us a whale could be tracked across oceans, he now swears out an affidavit that whales can be recognized as individuals, can be famous, and can sink ships — because otherwise readers might 'scout at Moby Dick as a monstrous fable, or still worse and more detestable, a hideous and intolerable allegory.' I love that sentence. Melville is more afraid of being read as allegory than as lie. He wants the whale to be a whale first.

So the evidence: harpoons with the same private mark recovered from the same whale three years apart; named whales — Timor Tom, New Zealand Jack, Morquan, Don Miguel — 'as well known to the students of Cetacean History as Marius or Sylla'; and then the ship Essex, stove in by a whale in 1820, the real disaster this novel grew from. Ishmael has met Owen Chase, read his narrative, talked to his son. The chapter is a bibliography of the book's own origins.

But the line I think about most is in the middle, thrown at the reader over breakfast: 'For God’s sake, be economical with your lamps and candles! not a gallon you burn, but at least one drop of man’s blood was spilled for it.' The whole grand fishery, the whole voyage, exists so that people ashore can read at night. Melville is writing a book by whale-oil light about the men who died to provide it, and he stops to say so. And then, in the closing pages, the tone loosens — a sperm whale requests 'a few moments’ confidential business' with a skeptical commodore — and Ishmael's uncle turns up in Langsdorff's Voyages. The affidavit ends by proving that the marvels are old: Procopius's sea-monster in the sixth century was, he decides, a sperm whale too. Nothing new under the sun, including the thing that sinks you.

annotations.quote: For this is one of those disheartening instances where truth requires full as much bolstering as error.
annotations.note: Ishmael's complaint that facts need as much propping as lies. It's the affidavit's justification, and also a sly admission that the book's realism is a performance requiring witnesses.

annotations.quote: they might scout at Moby Dick as a monstrous fable, or still worse and more detestable, a hideous and intolerable allegory.
annotations.note: Melville's fear isn't that you'll disbelieve him but that you'll believe him symbolically. He wants a real whale. The Whiteness chapter three pages earlier made the whale a symbol of the void; here he snatches it back.

annotations.quote: Do you suppose that that poor fellow there, who this moment perhaps caught by the whale-line off the coast of New Guinea, is being carried down to the bottom of the sea by the sounding leviathan—do you suppose that that poor fellow’s name will appear in the newspaper obituary you will read to-morrow at your breakfast?
annotations.note: The reader at breakfast is confronted with a man drowning right now, unreported. It's the book's ethics compressed: the economy you live in kills people you'll never hear of.

annotations.quote: For God’s sake, be economical with your lamps and candles! not a gallon you burn, but at least one drop of man’s blood was spilled for it.
annotations.note: The single most direct address to the reader in the novel. Every page of Moby-Dick was read by whale-oil light in 1851, so the line is a bill presented to its own audience.

annotations.quote: I had no more idea of being facetious than Moses, when he wrote the history of the plagues of Egypt.
annotations.note: Landsmen laugh when he describes whales; he compares himself to Moses reporting plagues. The overstatement is funny, and it's also his real problem — the truth about whales sounds like a joke.

annotations.quote: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean.
annotations.note: This is the seed of the novel: the real Essex, rammed and sunk by a sperm whale. Melville read Owen Chase's narrative at sea and met Chase's son. The affidavit is where the book confesses its source.

annotations.quote: But he was stopped on the way by a portly sperm whale, that begged a few moments’ confidential business with him.
annotations.note: After the Essex, the tone drops to comedy — a whale requesting a meeting with a skeptical commodore. The alternation of horror and farce within a single chapter is Melville's signature, and here it's inside one paragraph.

annotations.quote: I have the honor of being a nephew of his.
annotations.note: Ishmael's uncle appears in a Russian travel narrative. Melville really did have an uncle, John D'Wolf, on that voyage. The line where narrator and author overlap most closely is buried in an affidavit about whales bumping ships.

annotations.quote: so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon—Verily there is nothing new under the sun.
annotations.note: The chapter that began as evidence for a modern marvel ends by insisting the marvel is ancient. Procopius's monster becomes a sperm whale by inference. Melville's proof of the whale's reality is that it has always been sinking ships.

links.why: The Affidavit supplies the documented cases behind the rumour-chapter's legend.
The Town-Ho's Story is the Affidavit in narrative form — a real-seeming case of Moby Dick acting like judgment.

links.q: from hell’s heart I stab at thee
links.why: The Essex, stove by a whale — the historical event the third day of the chase re-enacts.
